newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain '96 cash deficit to be distorted - Caruana.
newsitem.headline: Spain '96 cash deficit to be distorted - Caruana.

text.p: Spain will meet its 1996 target to have a public sector deficit at 4.4 percent of gross domestic product, but the cash deficit will be worse than first thought because of more than 1.2 trillion pesetas of extraordinary items.

Jaime Caruana, general director of the Spanish Treasury, told Reuters in an interview recorded for Reuters Financial Television that the cash deficit this year will be distorted by extraordinary items, but he made clear these will not have an effect on the Maastricht criteria.
"This year's cash deficit is artificial, given distortions from extraordinary items," Caruana said.
While the cash deficit would underperform initial expectations, the deficit on on a national account basis, relevant to the Maastricht criteria, was meeting or even outperforming expectations.
"We'll meet the 4.4-percent target," he said. "This (will) work perfectly. If it registers any difference to expectations, it's going to be narrower," he said referring to National Account criteria.
But the cash deficit, originally expected to be twenty percent less than in 1995, could now end the year 10-percent higher than in 1995.
"On a cash basis, we forecast a 20-percent reduction, and that's the equivalent of a 10-percent increase (given these extraordinary items)," he said.

The difference between the two deficit accounts stems from three extraordinary items. The first was the surprise hole in 1995 accounts discovered in July 1996 of 721 billion pesetas and 200 billion pesetas from fewer privatisations than originally forecast.
In addition, there are 151 billion pesetas from interest payments of the previous year and 143 billion pesetas from a change in accounting for interest expenditures.
In the first 10 months, the central government's accumulated deficit on a cash basis was 2.24 trillion pesetas.
Meanwhile, the deficit on a national account basis in the first 10 months of 1996 was at 1.78 trillion pesetas, or 2.4 percent of gross domestic product.
The difference between the two accounting measures will widen further this year.
